Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 29, verses 1–3:

Meccan [except from verse 1 to verse 11, which are Medinan], and its verses are 69 [it was revealed after al-Rum]. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The verb of opinion (al-husban, the verbs of thinking such as *hasiba* and *zanna*) cannot govern the individual words (mufradat) alone, but only the propositions (jumal). Do you not see that if you say:

"I thought Zayd and I supposed the horse," it means nothing until you say: "I thought Zayd knowledgeable and I supposed the horse swift." This is because your saying "Zayd is knowledgeable" or "the horse is swift" is a statement conveying a proposition. You wished to report that this proposition holds in your mind by way of supposition, not certainty. You could not express its holding in your mind in that manner except by mentioning both halves of the sentence, with the verb of opinion placed before them, so that your purpose is complete. If you ask: "Where is the statement conveying the proposition that the verb of opinion requires in the verse?" I answer: it is in His saying ﴿أَنْ يُتْرَكُوا أَنْ يَقُولُوا آمَنَّا وَهُمْ لا يُفْتَنُونَ﴾ [that they will be left alone because they say, "We believe," and they will not be tested]. Its implied sense is: "Do they suppose that their being left untested, because of their saying 'We believe,' ..." So *al-tark* (leaving) is the first object of *hasiba*, and their saying "We believe" is the predicate (khabar). As for "untested" (ghayr maftunin), it completes the *tark*, because it is from *tark* in the sense of *tasyir* (making something into a state), as in the verse:

"So I left him, the beasts of prey tearing at him" [the explanation of this line was given in the first volume, page 75, so refer to it if you wish; its corrector].

Do you not see that before bringing in the verb of opinion, you can say: "He left them untested because of their saying, 'We believe,'" by estimating: "established and settled," before the lam? If you ask: "*An yaqulu* (that they say) is the cause of their being left untested; how then can it be the predicate of a subject?" I answer: just as you say "his going out for fear of harm" and "his striking for discipline," where discipline and fear were two causes in your saying "I went out for fear of harm" and "I struck him for discipline." And you may also say: "I thought his going out for fear of harm, and I supposed his striking for discipline," making them two objects, just as you made them subject and predicate.

*Al-fitnah* (trial, testing) means examination through severe obligations: leaving one's homeland, striving against enemies, all difficult acts of obedience, abstaining from desires and pleasures, and through poverty, famine, and various calamities to one's person and property, and by enduring the unbelievers' harm, plots and injury. The meaning is: Do those who have uttered the testimony of faith with their tongues and displayed the claim of belief suppose that they will be left with this alone, untested? Rather, Allah will test them with various kinds of trials, until He tries their patience, the steadiness of their feet, the soundness of their beliefs, and the purity of their intentions, so that the sincere is distinguished from the insincere, the firm in religion from the wavering, and the established from the worshipper who is on the edge (of faith), as He said: ﴿لَتُبْلَوُنَّ فِي أَمْوالِكُمْ وَأَنْفُسِكُمْ وَلَتَسْمَعُنَّ مِنَ الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الْكِتابَ مِنْ قَبْلِكُمْ وَمِنَ الَّذِينَ أَشْرَكُوا أَذىً كَثِيراً وَإِنْ تَصْبِرُوا وَتَتَّقُوا فَإِنَّ ذلِكَ مِنْ عَزْمِ الْأُمُورِ﴾ [You will surely be tested in your possessions and your persons, and you will surely hear from those who were given the Book before you and from those who associate partners with Allah much hurtful speech. But if you are patient and mindful of Allah, indeed that is among the matters requiring resolve].

It is related that the verses were revealed concerning some of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who had become distressed by the harm of the polytheists. It was also said concerning Ammar ibn Yasir, who was tortured for the sake of Allah. And it was said: concerning some people who had embraced Islam in Mecca. The emigrants wrote to them: "Your Islam will not be accepted until you emigrate." So they set out, but the polytheists pursued them and turned them back. When the verses were revealed, they wrote them to them, so they set out, and the polytheists pursued them and fought them; some of them were killed and some escaped. It was also said: concerning Mihja' ibn Abdullah, the freed slave of Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), who was the first Muslim to be killed on the day of Badr. Amir ibn al-Hadrami shot him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The master of the martyrs is Mihja', and he is the first of this community to be called to the gate of Paradise." [Al-Tha'labi related it from Muqatil, who said: "These two verses were revealed concerning Mihja' ibn Abdullah, the freed slave of Umar, who was the first of the Muslims to be killed on the day of Badr. Amir ibn al-Hadrami shot him with an arrow and killed him. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'The master of the martyrs is Mihja', and he is the first of this community to be called to the gate of Paradise.' Its chain to Muqatil is at the beginning of his book. In Ibn Abi Shaybah's *al-Dala'il*, through the route of al-Qasim ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, he said: 'The first to be martyred at Badr was Mihja', the freed slave of Umar.'] His parents and his wife grieved over him.

﴿وَلَقَدْ فَتَنَّا﴾ [And We certainly tested] is connected to "Do they suppose" or to "they will not be tested," like your saying: "Will such-and-such not be tested, when someone better than him has been tested?" The meaning is that the followers of the Prophets (peace be upon them) before them were afflicted with trials and tribulations similar to what afflicted them, or worse, and they endured, as He said: ﴿وَكَأَيِّنْ مِنْ نَبِيٍّ قاتَلَ مَعَهُ رِبِّيُّونَ كَثِيرٌ فَما وَهَنُوا﴾ [And how many a prophet fought, along with him many godly people, and they did not falter] ... the verse. And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Those before you were seized, and a saw was placed on the head of one of them and he was split into two halves, and that did not turn him from his religion; and his flesh and sinews were combed with iron combs, down to the bone, and that did not turn him from his religion." [Al-Bukhari related it from the hadith of Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, and it is more complete than this.]

﴿فَلَيَعْلَمَنَّ اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ صَدَقُوا وَلَيَعْلَمَنَّ الْكاذِبِينَ﴾ [So Allah will surely make known those who are truthful, and He will surely make known the liars]: through the testing, He will know those who were truthful in belief and those who lied in it. If you ask: "How, when He has known that from eternity?" I answer: He has always known it as a non-existent thing, and He does not know it as existing except when it comes into existence. [Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "If you say: He has always known the truthful and the liars before the testing, what is the meaning of this statement? I say: He has always known it as non-existent, and He does not know it as existing except when it comes into existence." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: What he mentioned gives the impression of an unsound doctrine, namely the belief that knowledge of what exists is different from knowledge of what will be. The truth is that the knowledge of Allah the Exalted is one, and it relates to the existing thing at the time of its existence, before it and after it, as it is. The benefit of mentioning knowledge here, though it precedes the existence of the known, is to alert, through the cause, to the effect, which is the recompense. It is as if He, exalted is He, said: "We will know them, so We will recompense them according to His knowledge of them." And Allah knows best.]

The meaning is: the sincere among them will surely be distinguished from the liar. It is also permissible that this be a promise and a threat, as if He said: "He will surely reward those who are truthful, and He will surely punish the liars."

And Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) and al-Zuhri read *wa-liya'lamanna* (from *i'lam*, causing to know), meaning: and Allah will make the people know who they are, or He will mark them with a sign by which people will recognize them, from the whiteness and blackness of faces, and the kohl and blueness of eyes.

Passage: "أَنْ يَسْبِقُونا" — "that they would outrun us," meaning: that they would escape us. The sense is that the requital will overtake them without fail, and they had not hoped to escape nor entertained the thought of it; rather, out of heedlessness, little reflection on the outcome, and persistence in sins, they are in the form of one who is capable of that and hopes for it. Its parallel is ﴿And you cannot escape [Allah] on the earth﴾ [29:22], and ﴿And let not those who disbelieve think that they have outrun [Us]. Indeed, they cannot escape﴾ [8:59].

If you say: where are the two objects of "ḥasiba" (to think/suppose)? I say: the clause introduced by "an" (that), consisting of a predicate and its subject, takes the place of the two objects, like His saying, ﴿Or do you think that you will enter Paradise﴾ [2:214]. It is also permissible that ḥasiba be taken to carry the meaning of qaddara (to assume), and that "am" (or) be disjunctive (munqaṭi'ah).

The sense of the disjunction (al-iḍrāb) in it is: this supposition is more false than the first supposition, because that one assumes that he will not be tested regarding his faith, whereas this one thinks that he will not be requited for his evil deeds. ﴿Evil is what they judge﴾ [29:4] — evil is that which they judge, their judgment this. Or: evil is the judgment they pass, their judgment this, and the object of the dispraise has been omitted.

Liqa' Allah (the meeting with God): a figure of speech for reaching the final outcome, namely meeting the Angel of Death, the Resurrection, the Reckoning, and the Recompense.

That state is likened to the state of a servant who comes before his master after a long absence, while the master has been informed of what he used to do and neglect. Either the master receives him with cheerfulness and welcome, because he is pleased with his deeds, or he receives him with the opposite, because he is displeased with them. So the meaning of His words, ﴿Whoever hopes for the meeting with God﴾, is: whoever hopes for that state, and that in it he will receive honour from God and cheerful welcome. ﴿Then the term of God﴾, which is death, ﴿is surely coming﴾ without doubt. So let him hasten to righteous deeds that make his hope true, fulfil his expectation, and earn through them nearness to God and closeness to Him. ﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾, nothing hidden from Him of what His servants say or do, so He is worthy of piety and fear.

It has been said that yarju (ﻳَﺮْﺟُﻮ) means "fears," from the saying of al-Hudhali describing a honey-gatherer:

*When the stinging insects sting him, he does not fear their sting, and he allies himself with them in the house of the hives, the honeycombs.*

This is a verse of Abu Dhu'ayb, describing a man who gathers honey: that when the dabr (stinging insects, with the vowel either fatha or kasra) — meaning the male bees and the wasps — sting him...

It is also transmitted as "lam yarj" (he did not fear), meaning: he did not fear their sting when they intended to sting him. Or: they stung him in fact, and he did not fear such a thing from them, or did not anticipate it or take heed of it. And "hālafahā" means he kept company with them. It is also narrated with a dotted letter (khā'), meaning he opposed their intention, or came after them once they had gone out to forage.

Al-nawb: a kind of bee, its singular being nā'ib, because it goes to its hive turn after turn. ʿawāsil: abounding in honey. It is also narrated as ʿawāmil, with the letter mīm, because they produce honey.

If you say: "Surely the term of God is coming; how does it fall as the answer to the condition?" I say: when it is known that by "the meeting with God" is meant that figurative state, and the time in which that state occurs is the appointed term of death, then it is as if he said: "Whoever hopes for the meeting with God, then the meeting with God is coming, because the appointed term is the time in which the meeting occurs," just as you say: "Whoever hopes to meet the king, then Friday is near," when it is known that he sits with the people on Friday.

And whoever strives against his own self, restraining it from what it commands him and compelling it toward what it refuses, then he only strives for its benefit, because the benefit of that returns to it. God, Mighty and Majestic is He, commands and forbids only out of mercy toward His servants, while He is Self-Sufficient above them and above their obedience.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 29, verse 7:

Either it refers to righteous Muslim people who have committed some wrongdoings in their deeds, whose misdeeds are overshadowed by their good deeds, so He expiates them for them, that is, He removes their punishment by the reward of good deeds, and He recompenses them with the best of what they used to do, that is, the best recompense for their deeds. Or it refers to polytheists who believed and did righteous deeds, so Allah, Mighty and Majestic, expiates their misdeeds by removing the punishment for the disbelief and sins they committed before, and He recompenses them with the best recompense for their deeds in Islam. [[Mahmud said: "By these people is meant one of two groups: either Muslim people whose misdeeds are minor sins overshadowed by good deeds, or people who believed and did righteous deeds after disbelief, for Islam erases what came before it." Ahmad said: He has restricted the vast mercy of Allah, the Exalted, based on his corrupt principle regarding the obligation of the divine threat (wa'id, the threat of punishment) upon the perpetrator of major sins unless he repents. He stated the expiation of minor sins absolutely, even without repentance, when good deeds overshadow them. Both principles are Qadari (a school denying divine predestination) and to be avoided. And Allah is the Granter of success.]].

«Wassa» (wassā, to enjoin) has the same ruling and the same range of usage as «amara» (to command). One says: "I enjoined Zayd to do good" (wassaytu Zaydan bi-an yafʿala khayran), just as you say: "I commanded him to do it" (amartuhu bi-an yafʿala). From this is the line of verse from *Islah al-Mantiq* (*Reform of Speech*, by Ibn al-Sikkit):

*And a woman of the Dhubyan enjoined her sons*
*that they should strike the coverlets and the leather bags.*

[[The poet is Mu'aqqar ibn Himar al-Bariqi. Ibn al-Sikkit recited it in his book titled *Islah al-Mantiq*. That is, a woman attributed to the tribe of Dhubyan enjoined her sons. *An* is the light form of the heavy *inna*, and its noun is the *dhamir al-sha'n* (the pronoun of the matter), and its predicate is *kadhaba*, which may also mean "it became obligatory," as in *al-Sihah* (*The Sihah*, the lexicon of al-Jawhari). In a hadith: "Three journeys have become obligatory upon you" (kadhbana), that is, became obligatory. And from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him: "The Hajj has become obligatory upon you" (kadhaba), that is, became obligatory. The sentence carries the sense of urging and inciting. *Al-qarathif* is the plural of *qarfaf*, which is a velvet quilt. *Al-quruf* are leather containers in which roasted meat is placed. *Al-qarf* (with a kasra) is the peeled skin. *Al-qarfa* is a bark used for treatment. *Al-qarf* (with a fatha) is a leather container tanned with *qarfa*. *Iqtarafa* and *iqtaraba* are close in both form and meaning, that is, she enjoined them to seize them and to keep them with themselves.]]

It is as if she said: "I commanded them to plunder them." From this is the verse ﴿And Abraham enjoined it upon his sons﴾ (2:132), that is, he enjoined them with the word of monotheism and commanded them with it. Your saying "I enjoined Zayd concerning ʿAmr" means: I enjoined him to take charge of ʿAmr's affairs, to look after him, and similar things. Likewise the meaning of ﴿And We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents﴾ (29:8) is: We enjoined him to show kindness to his parents, or to bestow goodness upon his parents, that is, an act that is good, or something that is in itself good because of its great goodness, like His saying ﴿and speak to people with goodness﴾ (2:83). It has been recited as *husnan* and as *ihsanan*. It is permissible to take *husnan* as an instance of your saying "Zayd!" with the verb "strike" implied, when you see someone ready to strike, so you put him in the accusative by implying a verb: "Do good to the two of them" (awli-humā) or "Do good to them both" (ifʿal bihimā), because enjoining them is indicative of it, and what follows corresponds to it, as if he said: "We said: do good to them both, and ﴿do not obey them in associating partners with Me﴾ (29:8) if they urge you to it." According to this interpretation, if one pauses at *biwalidayh* and begins with *husnan*, the pause is sound; but according to the first interpretation, it is necessary to imply the verb "We said," meaning: "And We said: if they strive with you, O human being, to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge," that is, you have no knowledge of its divinity. The intended meaning of the negation of knowledge is the negation of the known, as if He said: "to associate with Me something which cannot properly be a god." The meaning is: He enjoined him concerning his parents and commanded him to show kindness to them, then, by His prohibition of obeying them when they urge him to what was mentioned, He alerted that every right, however great, is void when the right of Allah comes, and that there is no obedience to a created being in disobedience to the Creator. Then He said: ﴿To Me is your return, all of you, those who believed among you and those who associated partners﴾ (cf. 29:8), so I will recompense you with the full recompense. In this are two matters. The first: the recompense is with Me, so do not entertain in your soul any harshness toward your parents or disobedience to them because of their polytheism, and do not deprive them of your goodness and kindness in this world, just as I do not withhold My provision from them. The second: a warning against following them in polytheism, and an urging to steadfastness and uprightness in religion through mention of the return and the threat.

It is related that Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas al-Zuhri, may Allah be pleased with him, when he embraced Islam, his mother, who was Hamna bint Abi Sufyan ibn Umayya ibn ʿAbd Shams, said: "O Saʿd, it has reached me that you have turned away from your religion. By Allah, I will not let the shade of a roof of a house, or the sun and the wind, reach me, and food and drink are forbidden to me until you disbelieve in Muhammad." She was the dearest of her children to her. Saʿd refused, and she remained like that for three days. Then Saʿd came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and complained to him, so this verse was revealed, along with the one in Luqman and the one in al-Ahqaf, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded him to be patient with her and to seek her pleasure through kindness. [[Al-Wahidi, al-Tha'labi and al-Waqidi mentioned it thus, without a chain of narration (isnad). The story is in Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, in a context other than this.]]

It is also related that it was revealed concerning ʿAyyash ibn Abi Rabiʿa al-Makhzumi. That was because he emigrated together with ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with both of them, as close companions, until they alighted in Madina. Then Abu Jahl ibn Hisham and al-Harith ibn Hisham, his two maternal brothers, whose mother was Asma bint Makhrama, a woman from Banu Tamim of Banu Hanzala, went out, alighted with ʿAyyash, and said to him: "Indeed, among the religion of Muhammad is maintaining the ties of kinship and kindness to parents. Your mother has left off eating, drinking and seeking shelter in a house until she sees you, and she loves you more than we do. So come out with us." And they wormed their way into him by cunning [[His saying "and they wormed their way into him in the crest and the back" (wa-fatalā minhu fi'l-dhurwa wa'l-ghārib): in *al-Sihah*: "So-and-so kept wheedling against so-and-so in the crest and the back," that is, he kept circling around him by means of his deception.]]. ʿAyyash consulted ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "They are deceiving you, but I swear to you that I will divide my wealth between myself and you." But they kept at him until he obeyed them and disobeyed ʿUmar. So ʿUmar said to him: "Since you have disobeyed me, take my she-camel, for there is no camel in the world that can overtake her. If you have any doubt about them, turn back." When they reached the wilderness, Abu Jahl said:

"Indeed, my camel has become exhausted, so carry me with you."

He said: "Yes." So he [ʿAyyash] dismounted to make it kneel for himself and for him [Abu Jahl]. They seized him, bound him tightly, and each of them lashed him one hundred times, then they took him to his mother. She said: "You will remain in torment until you turn back from the religion of Muhammad." Then this was revealed.

in the company of the righteous (fi al-salihin): among them as a whole. Righteousness (al-salah) is among the most eloquent attributes of the believers, and it is the wish of God's prophets. God Almighty said, relating of Solomon (peace be upon him): ﴿And admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants﴾. And He said of Abraham (peace be upon him): ﴿And indeed, in the Hereafter he will be among the righteous﴾. Or it means "in the entrance of the righteous," which is Paradise. This is similar to the words of God Almighty: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger – those are with the ones on whom Allah has bestowed favor﴾, the verse.

Zamakhshari's commentary (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 29, verses 10–11:

They are people who used to believe with their tongues. When they suffer harm from the disbelievers, which is what is meant by "the trial of people," that becomes a diversion for them from faith, just as the punishment of God is a diversion for the believers from disbelief, or as the punishment of God ought to be a diversion. And when God gives victory to the believers and they gain spoils, they approach them and say, ﴿Indeed, we were with you﴾, meaning: following you in your religion, steadfast upon it as you are steadfast, ﴿no one could have tried us﴾, ﴿so give us our share of the spoils﴾. Then He, glory be to Him, informs that He is ﴿most knowing of what is in the breasts of the worlds﴾, meaning the worlds know what is in their breasts, and among that is what the breasts of these people conceal of hypocrisy. This is a disclosure by Him to the believers of what they hid inwardly. Then He promised the believers and threatened the hypocrites. And it was read: "wa-la-yaqulunna" (ليقولنّ), with a fatha on the lam.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 29, verses 12–13:**

They commanded them to follow their path (*sabil*), which is their way of life in their religion, and they commanded themselves to bear their sins. So the second command is conjoined to the first (*'atf al-amr 'ala al-amr*), and their meaning was: let these two things be combined in attainment, that you follow our path and that you bear your sins. The meaning is that bearing the burden is made conditional upon following. This is the statement of the chieftains of Quraysh, who said to those among them who had believed: "We will not be resurrected, nor will you. If that should happen, then we will bear your sin on your behalf." We also see among those who call themselves Muslims someone who follows those people: when he wants to encourage his companion to commit some grave sin, he says: "Do this, and its sin is upon my neck." How many are deceived by such a guarantee from the weak and ignorant among the common people! Among such stories is what is related: a man from *ahl al-hashw* (the lay literalists) presented his needs to Abu Ja'far al-Mansur. When al-Mansur had fulfilled them, the man said: "O Commander of the Faithful, one great need remains." He said: "And what is it?" He said: "Your intercession on the Day of Resurrection." Then Amr ibn Ubayd, may God have mercy on him, said to him: "Beware of these people, for they are highwaymen in a place of safety."

[[Mahmud said: "Some of those who call themselves Muslims, when they want to encourage their companion to commit a sin, say to him: 'Do this, and its sin is upon my neck.' Among such stories is what is related: a man presented his needs to al-Mansur, and when he had fulfilled them, he said: 'O Commander of the Faithful, there remains for me a need of yours, which is the greatest.' He said: 'And what is it?' He said: 'Your intercession at the gathering (al-mahshar).' Then Amr said: 'O Commander of the Faithful, beware of these people, for they are highwaymen in a place of safety.'"

Ahmad said: Amr ibn Ubayd was the first of the Qadariyya (*al-Qadariyya*) to deny intercession, so beware of him. The verse does not correspond to the anecdote, but al-Zamakhshari builds upon the view that there is no difference between believing in intercession and believing that the disbelievers bear the sins of their followers, and therefore he placed the two in one line. We seek refuge in God from that.

As for His saying ﴿Indeed, they are liars﴾, there is a fine point from which one may derive evidence for the validity of the imperative being used in the sense of a declarative statement (*majii' al-amr bi-ma'na al-khabar*). For some people denied this and insisted on explaining all that is reported in this regard as retaining the original sense of the imperative. This did not succeed for them in this verse, because God, exalted is He, followed their saying ﴿and let us bear your sins﴾, which is in the form of an imperative, with ﴿Indeed, they are liars﴾, and falsehood (*al-takdhib*) applies only to declarative statements.]]

If you say: How did He call them liars, when they only guaranteed something which God knew they would not be able to fulfill? One who guarantees something whose power to fulfill it is not known is not called a liar, neither at the time of guaranteeing nor at the time of inability, because in both states he does not fall under the definition of the liar, who is one who informs about a thing not as it actually is. I say: God likened their condition, since He knew that what they had guaranteed had no path by which they could fulfill it, so their guarantee, in His estimation, was not as the guaranteed matter actually is. Therefore He described them as liars, those whose information about the matter was not as it actually is. It is also permissible that He means they are liars because they said that while their hearts were contrary to it, like the liars who make promises while intending to break them.

﴿And they will surely bear their own burdens﴾, meaning the burdens of themselves, ﴿and burdens along with their burdens﴾, meaning other burdens besides the sins they had guaranteed to the believers to bear, namely the burdens of those who were a cause of their misguidance. ﴿And they will surely be questioned﴾, a questioning of rebuke, ﴿concerning what they used to fabricate﴾, meaning what they used to invent of lies and falsehoods.

It has been recited: *min khatiyyatihim* (from their sins).

The age of Noah, peace be upon him, was one thousand and fifty years. He was sent as a prophet at forty, remained among his people nine hundred and fifty years, and lived sixty years after the Flood. According to Wahb, he lived one thousand four hundred years.

If you ask: why was it not said "nine hundred and fifty years," as you have put it? I answer: what God revealed is more wise. For if it had been said as you say, it could have been supposed that this number was applied to its larger part, and this supposition is removed by its coming in this form. It is as if it had been said: "nine hundred and fifty full years, complete in number." But that form is more concise, more pleasing in expression, and fuller in benefit. [Mahmud said: "He turned away from 'nine hundred and fifty' because in that form it allows the number to be applied to its larger part, unlike its coming with an exception." Ahmad said: "Because the exception is a corrective return upon the whole sentence by reducing it, to fix the number precisely, so it does not allow exaggeration, since exaggeration is not permissible with an exact number."]

There is another subtle point: the story is brought to mention what Noah, peace be upon him, was afflicted with by his people and what he endured of long patience, as consolation for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and as strengthening for him. So mentioning the round number, beyond which there is no larger round number, is more effective and better reaches the purpose of making the listener feel the length of his period of patience. [Mahmud said: "There is another subtle point: the story is brought to mention what Noah endured of long patience, as consolation to him, peace be upon him. So mentioning the round number beyond which there is no larger one is more effective for the purpose. He said: 'He varied the two expressions, mentioning 'years' (sanah) first and 'a year' ('am) second, to avoid a repetition that is not praised except for the purpose of exaltation or glorification.'" Ahmad said: "If the excepted part were magnified, that would return with some magnification of the excepted-from part and its enlargement in the hearer's mind, and God knows best."]

If you ask: why did the specifying noun (tamyiz) come first as "years" (sanah) and second as "year" ('am)? I answer: because repeating the same word within one utterance is to be avoided in eloquence, unless that occurs for a purpose the speaker intends, such as magnification, awe-inspiring effect, or emphasis, or the like.

Al-Tufan is that which surrounds and encompasses with abundance and overpowering force, whether a flood, the darkness of night, or the like. Al-Ajjaj said:

"And the darkness-tufan covered the thick-leaved acacia" [In the verse: "Until, when its day was pouring down... and the darkness-tufan covered the thick-leaved acacia," said by al-Ajjaj describing a wild cow. Ma here is superfluous (za'idah). It is also reported as 'amma, with the unpointed letter and with the pointed letter, and the two meanings are close. Al-Tufan is everything that circles around a thing and encompasses it, of darkness, water, or the like. Al-Athab is a kind of tree resembling the fig tree; its singular is athabah. Attributing the pouring down to the day is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli) by way of ascribing the act to the time, or it is on the assumption of a specifying noun, meaning: it poured down rain, and the darkness of the trees in which it was concealed covered it.]

The companions of the ship were seventy-eight persons, half of them men and half of them women. Among them were Noah's sons: Sam, Ham, and Japheth, and their wives. According to Muhammad ibn Ishaq, they were ten: five men and five women. It has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "they were eight: Noah, his household, and his three sons." [Already mentioned in Hud.]

The pronoun in "We made it" refers either to the ship or to the event and the story.

Al-Tufan is that which surrounds and encompasses with abundance and overpowering force, whether a flood, the darkness of night, or the like. Al-Ajjaj said:

"And the darkness-tufan covered the thick-leaved acacia" [In the verse: "Until, when its day was pouring down... and the darkness-tufan covered the thick-leaved acacia," said by al-Ajjaj describing a wild cow. Ma here is superfluous (za'idah). It is also reported as 'amma, with the unpointed letter and with the pointed letter, and the two meanings are close. Al-Tufan is everything that circles around a thing and encompasses it, of darkness, water, or the like. Al-Athab is a kind of tree resembling the fig tree; its singular is athabah. Attributing the pouring down to the day is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli) by way of ascribing the act to the time, or it is on the assumption of a specifying noun, meaning: it poured down rain, and the darkness of the trees in which it was concealed covered it.]

The companions of the ship were seventy-eight persons, half of them men and half of them women. Among them were Noah's sons: Sam, Ham, and Japheth, and their wives. According to Muhammad ibn Ishaq, they were ten: five men and five women. It has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "they were eight: Noah, his household, and his three sons." [Already mentioned in Hud.]

The pronoun in "We made it" refers either to the ship or to the event and the story.

Zamakhshari's commentary (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 29, verses 16–18:

The word ﴿Ibrahim﴾ is in the accusative (naṣb) by an implied verb, "remember" (udhkur). Idh ("when") replaces it as a badal al-ishtimal (a substitution of inclusion, where the substituted term contains the thing it replaces), because times include what occurs within them. Alternatively, ﴿Ibrahim﴾ is coordinated (ma'ṭūf) with ﴿Nuh﴾, and idh is an adverb (ẓarf) governed by "We sent" (arsalna). The meaning is: We sent him when he reached a stage of age and knowledge at which he was fit to admonish his people, advise them, present the truth to them, and command them to worship and piety.

Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on them both, read ﴿Ibrahim﴾ in the nominative (raf'), meaning: "And among the messengers is Ibrahim."

﴿If you only knew﴾ means: if there is knowledge among you of what is better for you than what is worse for you. Or: if you looked with the seeing eye of insight rather than the blind eye of ignorance, you would know that it (worship of God) is better for you.

It is read: ﴿takhluqūna﴾ (you create) from khalaqa, in the intensive sense of creating much. And ﴿takhalluqūna﴾ (you fabricate), from takhalluqa, meaning "to lie and invent falsehood."

It is read: ﴿ifkan﴾ (a lie). This has two possibilities. It may be a verbal noun (maṣdar), like kadhdhaba (to lie) and la'iba (to play), and al-ifk is its lightened form, like al-kadhib and al-la'ib from their roots. Or it may be an adjective of the pattern fi'l, meaning "a creation of falsehood," i.e., one possessing falsehood and nonsense.

Their fabrication of falsehood (ikhtilaquhum al-ifk) is their naming of the idols as gods and as associates of God, or as intercessors with Him. Or the idols themselves are called ifk, and their making and carving of them is "creating falsehood."

If you ask: why was ﴿rizq﴾ (provision) made indefinite and then definite? I answer: because he intended, "They do not have the power to provide you with any sustenance at all," and then said, "so seek provision entirely from God," for He alone is the Provider, and He provides no one else. ﴿To Him you will be returned﴾.

It is read with an open ta' (﴿turja'ūna﴾ as tarjī'ūna, with the verb in the active form). So prepare yourselves to meet Him by worshipping Him and thanking Him for His blessings.

﴿And if you deny me﴾: your denial will not harm me, for the messengers before me were denied by their peoples, and they did not harm them. Rather, they harmed themselves, when what befell them befell them because of their denial of the messengers.

As for the messenger, his mission is complete once he has delivered the clear message, which removes doubt, and that is his being accompanied by God's signs and miracles. Or: even if you consider me a liar among yourselves, I have in the other prophets a model and consolation, since they too were denied, and the messenger's duty is to convey, not to be believed or disbelieved.

This verse and the verses that follow, up to the words ﴿So the answer of his people was not but﴾, may be part of Ibrahim's speech to his people, peace and blessings of God be upon him. They may also be verses inserted in the middle of the story of Ibrahim, concerning the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the Quraysh.

If you ask: if these are the words of Ibrahim, what is meant by "the nations before him"? I answer: the people of Shith, Idris, Nuh, and others. The people of Nuh alone suffice as a nation, in the sense of many denying nations. Idris lived a thousand years among his people until he was raised up to heaven, and a thousand people believed in him according to the number of his years, while their descendants remained in denial.

It is recited ﴿yaraw﴾ with the letter ya' and with the letter ta'. Also ﴿yubdi'﴾ and ﴿yubda'﴾ (both meaning "He originates"). Rather, it is an independent report of the repetition after death, just as the looking in His saying ﴿Look how He originated creation, then God produces the last creation﴾ falls on the origination and not on the production. A similar example is your saying: "I kept preferring so-and-so, and appointing him over whomever I appoint."

[Note by the commentator: "His saying 'yu'idhuhu' is not conjoined to 'yubdi'; it is an independent report, as in His saying 'how He originated creation, then God produces the last creation', like your saying: I kept preferring so-and-so and appointing him after me." Aḥmad said: He had earlier, at His saying ﴿Or who originates creation then repeats it﴾, held that it is conjoined, and he accepted the conjunction even though they deny the repetition, because acknowledging it is necessary for them. Here, however, he refused to make it conjoined. The difference, and God knows best, is that here, if the repetition were conjoined to the origination, it would fall under the past seeing, and that has not yet occurred. This is not the case in the verse of al-Naml. One might say: although it has not occurred, it is, by God's report of its occurrence, like something that has occurred and been seen, so it is treated as what has been seen and witnessed. But making it a second, separate report is clearer, and God knows best.]

If you ask: it is conjoined by a conjunctive particle, so it must have something it is conjoined to. What is that? I answer: it is the clause of His saying ﴿Have they not seen how God originates creation?﴾. Likewise, ﴿and I appoint him﴾ is conjoined to the clause of your saying "I kept preferring so-and-so." That refers to what His saying ﴿and it is easier for Him﴾ refers to in the meaning of ﴿yu'id﴾ (repeat). There is no difference between them except that the last is an origination after a similar origination, while the first is not like that.

It is also read ﴿al-nash'a﴾ and ﴿al-nash'ā'a﴾, like ﴿al-ra'fa﴾ and ﴿al-ra'āfa﴾ (both forms of "mercy/kindness").

If you ask: what is the meaning of explicitly naming Him, placing Him as a subject in His saying ﴿then God produces the last creation﴾, after referring to Him by a pronoun in His saying ﴿how He originated creation﴾? The expected form would have been: "how God originated creation, then He produces the last creation." I answer: the discourse with them was about the repetition, and it was at that point that the knees would knock together. When He established with them that the origination is from God, He argued against them that the repetition is an origination like the origination. So it is as if He said: "Then that One who produced the first creation is the One who produces the last creation." To indicate and draw attention to this meaning, He made His name prominent and placed it as the subject.

[Note by the editor: The explanation of this verse was given earlier in the second volume, page 563; refer to it if you wish.]

It may also mean: you cannot make Him incapable, wherever you descend into the depths and abysses of the earth, or ascend into the towers and fortresses that reach into the sky, as in His saying: ﴿And even if you were in towers built high﴾. Or it may mean: you cannot escape His command, which runs over the heavens and the earth, that it should be carried out upon you, so that He strikes you with a calamity that rises from the earth or descends from the heavens.

If you ask: what do you make of His saying, "Say: Travel in the earth"? I answer: it is a report of a speech that Abraham (peace be upon him) addressed to his people, just as our Messenger (ﷺ) relates God's speech in this manner in most of the Qur'an.

If you ask: if it is addressed to Quraysh, what is the purpose of its placement between the two ends of the story of Abraham and the sentence? Or must interpolated sentences be connected to what they interrupt? Do you not see that you would not say: "Mecca, and Zayd his father is standing, is the best of God's lands"? I answer: the mention of Abraham's story is intended only to relieve the Messenger of God (ﷺ) of his distress and to console him, and to show him that his father Abraham, the Friend of God, was afflicted with something of the same kind as what afflicted him, namely the polytheism of his people and their worship of idols. This, as you see, is an interjection that is well placed and connected. Then the remaining verses that follow it are its appendages and consequences, because they speak of monotheism and its proofs, the demolition of polytheism and the weakening of its foundations, the attribute of God's power and dominion, and the clarity of His proof and argument.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 29, verse 24:

It is recited as "jawāba qawmihi" in both the accusative (naṣb) and the nominative (raf'). [They said] "qālū" (they said): some of them said to others, or one of them said it while the rest were content, so they were all, in ruling, among the sayers. It is related that the fire did not benefit anyone on that day, meaning the day Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was thrown into the fire, and that was because its heat had gone.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 29, verse 25:

It is read in the accusative (naṣb), both without and with an annexed genitive (iḍāfa), and likewise in the nominative (rafʿ). The accusative has two readings. The first is as a causal clause (ʿalā al-taʿlīl), meaning: "so that you may love one another and keep bonds with one another," because you gather together in worshipping them, agree upon them, and are united, just as people agree upon a doctrine, and that becomes the cause of their mutual affection and friendship. The second is that it is a second object (mafʿūl thānī), as in His saying ﴿Has he seen him who has taken his own desire as his god?﴾ (Q. 45:23), meaning: you have taken the idols as a cause of affection between you, with the omission of an annexed noun (al-muḍāf) understood.

Or [the reading is] "you have taken them as affection between you," in the sense of "objects of affection between you" (maddūda), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among the people are those who take, besides Allah, rivals whom they love as they love Allah﴾ (Q. 2:165).

In the nominative there are two possibilities. It may be the predicate of inna, with mā understood as a relative pronoun (mawṣūla). Or it may be the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada' maḥdhūf). The meaning is: "the idols are affection between you," that is, "objects of affection," or "a cause of affection."

From ʿĀṣim [it is transmitted]: "affection between you," with bayn-akum read with a fatḥa together with the annexation, just as it is read in ﴿Indeed, your bond has been severed﴾ (Q. 6:94), where bayn is read with a fatḥa and is the subject (fāʿil). Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, read: "idols; indeed affection between you in the life of this world," meaning: you show affection to one another through them, or you love them in the life of this world.

﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection, some of you will disown others and curse one another.﴾ Mutual cursing, hatred, and enmity will take place among you: the worshippers will curse one another, and the worshippers and the idols will curse one another, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they will become enemies to them and deniers of their worship﴾ (Q. 19:82).

Lot was the son of Abraham's sister, peace be upon them both, and he was the first to believe in him when he saw that the fire had not burned him. And he said, meaning Abraham: "Indeed, I am emigrating ﴿to my Lord﴾" from Kuthaa, which is in the lands of Kufa, to Harran, and then from there to Palestine. For this reason they said: every prophet has an emigration, but Abraham had two emigrations. With him in his emigration were Lot, his wife Sarah, and Hagar, and he was seventy-five years old. ﴿To my Lord﴾: to where He commanded me to emigrate to Him. ﴿Indeed, He is the Mighty﴾: the One who protects me from my enemies; ﴿the Wise﴾: who does not command me except with what is in my interest.

His reward is the good praise, the sending of blessings upon him until the end of time, a righteous offspring, prophethood, and that all the religious communities (ahl al-milal) hold him in allegiance. If you ask: why was Isma'il (peace be upon him) not mentioned, while Ishaq and his descendants were mentioned?

I answer: He is indicated by His saying ﴿And We placed in his offspring prophethood and the Scripture﴾. The indication suffices because of the fame of his affair and the loftiness of his rank. If you ask: what is meant by "the Scripture" (al-kitab)? I answer: it is intended as the genus of scripture, so that there is included under it what was revealed to his descendants of the four books: the Torah, the Psalms, the Gospel, and the Qur'an.

Lūṭ (Lot) is in the conjunction with Ibrāhīm, or with what was conjoined to him. Al-fāḥishah is the act that is extreme in ugliness. "And no one among the worlds preceded you in it" is a resumed clause (jumlah mustaʾnafah) confirming the abominable nature of that act, as if a questioner had said: "Why was it an abomination?" It is answered: because no one before them undertook it, out of revulsion for it in their natures, given its extreme ugliness, until the people of Lūṭ undertook it, owing to the corruption of their clay and the foulness of their natures. They said: the male never mounted a male before the people of Lūṭ, ever.

It was also read as "innakum" without interrogation in the first and with it in the second. Abū ʿUbayda said: "I found it in the Imām with one letter, without a yāʾ, and I saw the second with two letters, the yāʾ and the nūn."

"And they cut off the way" (qaṭʿ al-sabīl): the work of highway robbers (qaṭṭāʿ al-ṭarīq), who kill souls and take wealth. It was also said: their waylaying travelers with the abomination.

From al-Ḥasan: "the cutting off of offspring by coming to what is not tillage."

"And [they committed] the evil (al-munkar)": from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allāh be pleased with them both, it is pelting with pebbles, shooting with pellets, snapping the fingers, chewing gum, using the miswak among people, undoing buttons, abuse, and obscenity in joking. From ʿĀʾishah, may Allāh be pleased with her: they used to commit tahābuq [[The commentator's note: in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, "al-ḥabq" with a kasra is "al-radām" (flatulence); and also "al-radām" with a ḍamma is "al-ḥabq." This is circular, so let its meaning be examined. Then I saw in the entry on "ḍaraṭa" that al-ḍarāṭ is al-radām, and one says ḍarata yaḍrubu ḍarṭan with a kasra on the zāy, like ḥabaqa yaḥbuqu ḥabqan. So al-taḥābuq is al-muḍārasah (mutual flatulence), as al-Nasafī expressed it. (ʿ)]].

It was also said: mockery of those who passed by them. It was said: openly displaying that deed in their assemblies. Every sin, its public display is uglier than concealing it; for this reason it came: "Whoever tears the veil of modesty, there is no backbiting for him." The gathering is called nādin only while its people are in it; when they rise from it, it is no longer a nādī.

"If you are among the truthful" in what you promise us of the descent of punishment. They used to corrupt people by driving them to the sins and abominations they were upon, willingly and unwillingly, and because they originated the abomination and established it as a practice for those after them. Allāh, exalted, said: "Those who disbelieved and barred from the way of Allāh, We increased their punishment upon punishment, because of what they used to corrupt" (Qurʾān 16:88). So Lūṭ, peace be upon him, wanted Allāh's wrath upon them to intensify, so he mentioned for that the attribute of corrupters in his supplication.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 29, verse 31–32:

By "bil-bushra" (with the good tidings) is meant the glad tidings of a son. "Al-nafila" (the grandson, an extra gift): these are Ishaq and Ya'qub. The idafa in "muhlikū" (its people who destroy) is an idafa of lightening (takhfif), not of definiteness (ta'rif). The meaning is the future tense. "Al-qarya" (the town) is Sodom, of which it was said: "Its judge is the worst of judges." "Kānū ẓālimīn" (they were wrongdoers) means that the wrongdoing had continued among them from their earlier days, and they were persistent in it. Their wrongdoing is their disbelief and their various sins. "Inna fīhā Lūṭan" (Indeed, in it is Lut) is not an informing of them that he was in it; rather it is an argument concerning his case, because when they gave as the reason for destroying its people their wrongdoing, he objected to them that in it is one who is innocent of wrongdoing. By the argument he intended: displaying compassion toward them, and what is incumbent upon the believer of grief for his brother, and of exerting himself in his support and protection, and of fear that harm or injury should touch him. Qatada said: "The believer does not see that he should not protect a believer. Do you not see their reply, that they know better than he who is in it?" They mean: we know better than you, and more informed about the condition of Lut and the condition of his people, and his distinction from them is a clear distinction, and that he does not deserve what they deserve, so be at ease in yourself and make the matter light for yourself. "La-nunajjiyannahu" (we will surely save him) has been recited with both the doubled and the single consonant, and likewise "munajjūka" (we will save you).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 29, verse 45:

Prayer (ṣalāh) becomes a *lutf* (a divine grace that inclines the worshipper toward obedience and away from disobedience) in abandoning sins, so it is as though it forbids them. If you ask: how many a worshipper commits sins while his prayer does not restrain him? I answer: the prayer that is prayer in the sight of God, the one for which reward is due, is that in which a person enters having first made a sincere repentance (*tawbah naṣūḥ*) and being God-fearing, in accordance with His saying ﴿Indeed, God accepts only from the God-fearing﴾ (5:27). He performs it with humble submission (*khushūʿ*) of the heart and the limbs. It is related from Ḥātim: "It is as though my feet are on the bridge (*ṣirāt*), Paradise is on my right, the Fire is on my left, the Angel of Death is above me, and I pray between fear and hope." Then he safeguards it after performing it, so that it is not rendered void. This is the prayer that forbids indecency and wrongdoing.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both: "Whoever his prayer does not command him to good and does not forbid him from evil, his prayer has only increased him in distance from God." [[Al-Ṭabarānī transmitted it through the narration of al-ʿAlāʾ ibn al-Musayyib, from one he named, from Ibn ʿAbbās, in this form, as a *mawqūf* report (one ending with a Companion). Al-Ṭabarānī, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Mardawayh also transmitted it through the route of Layth from ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbās as a *marfūʿ* report (one traced to the Prophet). There is a parallel on the authority of Ibn ʿUmar, transmitted by al-Dāraquṭnī in his *Gharāʾib Mālik*. Its isnad includes Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī. Ibn Ḥibbān said: "It is not permissible to argue with him. He narrates from Mālik what has no basis." It was also transmitted by Aḥmad in *al-Zuhd* as a saying of Ibn Masʿūd, and by ʿAbd al-Razzāq, al-Ṭabarī and al-Bayhaqī in *al-Shuʿab* from a *mursal* report (one where the Successor omits the Companion) of al-Ḥasan.]] It is related from al-Ḥasan, may God have mercy on him: "Whoever his prayer does not restrain from indecency and wrongdoing, his is not a prayer, and it is a burden upon him."

It has been said: whoever is attentive to the prayer, that will lead him, in time, to cease from evil deeds. It is related that it was said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "So-and-so prays by day and steals by night." He said: "Indeed his prayer will restrain him." [[Aḥmad, Isḥāq, Ibn Ḥibbān, al-Bazzār and Abū Yaʿlā transmitted it through ʿĪsā ibn Yūnus, Wakīʿ and Mujāhid, from al-Aʿmash, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Abū Hurayrah, who said: A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "So-and-so prays at night, and when morning comes he steals." He said: "Indeed his prayer will restrain him." Al-Bazzār transmitted it through Ziyād al-Bakkāʾī, and Abū Yaʿlā through Abū Isḥāq al-Fazārī, both from al-Aʿmash, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Jābir. Al-Bazzār said: "There is a difference of report concerning it from al-Aʿmash: it is said that it was also related from him, from Abū Sufyān, from Jābir."]] It is also related that a young man from the Anṣār used to pray the prayers with him, yet he would leave no indecency without committing it. This was described to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: "Indeed his prayer will restrain him." Not long after, he repented. [[I have not found it.]]

In any case, the one attentive to the prayer must be further removed from indecency and wrongdoing than the one who is not attentive to it. Furthermore, how many worshippers are there whom the prayer restrains from indecency and wrongdoing? The wording does not require that not a single one of the worshippers departs from its ruling. It is like saying: "Zayd forbids wrongdoing." You do not mean that he forbids all wrongdoings; you mean that this quality is present in him and proceeds from him, without implying generality.

﴿And the remembrance of God is greater﴾: this means that for the prayer is greater than other acts of obedience, and it is named "the remembrance of God," as in His saying ﴿so hasten to the remembrance of God﴾ (62:9). He said "and the remembrance of God" so that it stands alone as the cause, as if He had said: "And the prayer is greater, because it is the remembrance of God." Or, the meaning is: "And the remembrance of God at the time of indecency and wrongdoing, and the remembrance of His prohibition of them and His threat against them, is greater, and so it is more fitting that it restrain than the subtle grace found in the prayer."

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both: "And the remembrance of God of you, with His mercy, is greater than your remembrance of Him through obedience." ﴿And God knows what you do﴾ of good and obedience, and He will reward you with the best reward.

**[Verse 46] "with that which is best"**: meaning, the best conduct, which is to meet roughness with gentleness and anger with restraint.

The sura is to be approached with patience, as He said: ﴿Repel [evil] with that which is better﴾ (41:34). The exception is ﴿except those who wrong﴾, those who go to excess in transgression and obstinacy, who do not accept advice and for whom gentleness is of no benefit, so harshness is used with them. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 29, verse 48:

﴿And you did not recite any book before it, nor did you write one with your right hand.﴾ No one ever knew you to recite a Book or to write. Had there been any such thing, that is, of recitation or writing, ﴿the falsifiers would have had cause for doubt﴾ — from among the People of the Book — and they would have said: "The one we find described in our books is unlettered; he neither writes nor reads, and this is not him." Or the idolaters of Makkah would have doubted and said: "Perhaps he learned it, or wrote it with his own hand." If you say:

Why did He call them "falsifiers" (mubtilun), when, had he not been unlettered, and they had said, "This is not the one we find in our books," they would have been truthful and correct? And would the people of Makkah not also have been right in their saying "Perhaps he learned it, or wrote it," since he is a man who reads and writes?

I say: He called them falsifiers because they disbelieved in him while he was unlettered, which is far from doubt. It is as if He said: these falsifiers, in their disbelief in him, would have doubted with the utmost doubt had he not been unlettered; but since he is neither a reader nor a writer, there is no basis for their doubt. Another point: all the other prophets, peace be upon them, were not unlettered, and it was obligatory to believe in them and in what they brought, because they were confirmed by the Wise One through miracles. Suppose he were a reader and writer: why then did they not believe in him from the same standpoint from which they believed in Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them? Moreover, those who were sent down (with revelation) were not themselves miracles, whereas this revelation is a miracle; so they are falsifiers in not believing in him while he is unlettered, and falsifiers too if they did not believe in him even were he not unlettered.

If you ask: what is the benefit of His words "with your right hand"? I say: mentioning the right hand, which is the limb with which writing is practised, is an added depiction of what was negated concerning him, namely that he was a writer. Do you not see that if you say in the affirmative, "I saw the Amir writing this letter with his right hand," it is more emphatic in establishing that he himself undertook the writing? Likewise in the negation.

﴿Rather, it is clear signs in the breasts of those who have been given knowledge﴾ — those who memorize it and preserve it. These are two of the distinctive features of the Qur'an: that its verses are clear proofs of its inimitability, and that it is preserved in the breasts, recited by most of the community openly, unlike other books, which were not miracles and were read only from manuscripts. From this is what has come in the description of this community: "Their breasts are their Gospels" (ṣudūruhum anājīluhum). [Narrated by al-Tabarani through the transmission of Sinan ibn al-Harith, from Ibrahim, from Alqamah, from Ibn Mas'ud, raised (to the Prophet ﷺ), in the course of a hadith. Al-Waqidi related in al-Ridda, from Isma'il ibn Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Rabi'ah, from his father, that a Jew from the people of Saba' called Nu'man, who was the most learned of the Jewish rabbis, mentioned a story in which there is a description of the Prophet ﷺ in a book sealed among them, and in it is this.]

﴿And none denies Our clear signs except the wrongdoers who are arrogant.﴾

It is recited as *āyah* (آية) and *āyāt* (آيات). They meant: "Why was a sign not sent down to him, like the she-camel of Salih and the table spread (*mā'idah*) of Isa, peace be upon them both, and the like?"

﴿Signs are only with God﴾. He sends down whichever He wills. And if He willed to send down what you propose, He would have done it.

﴿And I am only a warner﴾. I am charged with warning and making it clear, with what I have been given of signs. It is not for me to choose His signs over Him, saying, "Send down to me this sign rather than that sign," while I know that the purpose of a sign is the establishment of proof, and all signs are, in this respect, like one sign.

Then He said: ﴿Is it not sufficient for them﴾, a sign that suffices in place of all other signs, if they are seekers of the truth and not obstinate? It is ﴿this Qur'an﴾, whose recitation continues over them in every place and time. So there remains with them a lasting sign that does not vanish or fade away, unlike every sign that disappears after it has occurred and exists in one place but not another. Indeed, in a sign like this, present in every place and time until the end of time, there is ﴿mercy﴾, a great blessing that cannot be fully thanked, and ﴿a reminder for a people who believe﴾.

It has also been said: "Is it not sufficient for them," meaning the Jews, that We have sent down to you the Book recited to them, confirming what is in their hands of your description and the description of your religion. It has also been said that some Muslims came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with a shoulder blade on which they had written some of what the Jews were saying. When he looked at it, he threw it away and said: "Enough of folly for a people, or of misguidance for a people, that they turn away from what their Prophet has brought them to what someone other than their Prophet has brought." So this was revealed. [[Narrated by al-Tabari and Abu Dawud in al-Maraasil through the route of Yahya ibn Ja'dah: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was approached by a group of Muslims with a writing on a shoulder blade," and he mentioned something similar; the wording of al-Tabari is as in the original.]] The first interpretation that we mentioned is the correct one.

﴿God suffices as a witness between me and you﴾, that I have conveyed to you what I was sent with, and warned you, and that you have met me with denial and rejection. ﴿He knows what is in the heavens and the earth﴾, so He is aware of my affair and yours, and knows my truth and your falsehood.

﴿And those who believed in falsehood﴾ among you, which is what you worship besides God, ﴿and disbelieved in God and His signs, they are the losers﴾, those who are defrauded in their bargain, since they exchanged faith for disbelief. However, the speech comes in the manner of fairness, like His saying: ﴿And indeed, either we or you are upon guidance or in clear error﴾, and like the saying of Hassan:

*Fa-sharru-kumā li-khayri-kumā al-fidā'*
(So the evil of the two of you is the ransom for the good of the two of you)

It is also narrated that Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his companions said: "O Muhammad, who will bear witness for you that you are the Messenger of God?" So this was revealed.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 29, verse 56:

The meaning of the verse: when a believer finds that worship is not made easy for him in the land where he is, and the affairs of his religion do not proceed for him as he would like, then let him emigrate from it to a land which he judges to be one in which his heart is more secure, his religion sounder, his worship more abundant, and his humility better. By my life, the regions vary greatly in this respect. We have tested, and our predecessors tested, and among what we have traversed and what they have traversed we have found nothing more helpful for subduing the self, resisting desire, gathering a scattered heart, binding up a dispersed concern, encouraging contentment, driving away Satan, keeping far from many trials, and securing the religious affair in general, than dwelling in the Sacred Precinct of God and being near the House of God. So praise be to God for what He has made easy and near of that, and for what He has granted of patience and inspired of gratitude. And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever flees with his religion from one land to another, even if it is a span of land, has earned Paradise and will be the companion of Abraham and Muhammad." [[Al-Tha'labi narrated it from the mursal of al-Hasan, and it has been mentioned before in Surat al-Nisa.]] It was also said: this verse concerns the oppressed believers in Mecca, regarding whom the verse was revealed: ﴿Was not the earth of God spacious, so that you might emigrate therein?﴾. This was because the affair of their religion was not being settled for them among the disbelievers. ﴿So worship Me alone﴾.

In the first person, as in: ﴿Him I have struck﴾ ("iyyahu darabtuhu"); in the third person, and ﴿Iyyaka 'addatuka﴾ in the second person. The estimated form is: "fa-iyyaya fa-'budu" (so Me alone worship), i.e., "fa-'budun." If you say: what is the meaning of the fa' in ﴿fa-'budun﴾ and the fronting of the object? I say: the fa' is the response to an elided condition, because the meaning is: "Indeed My earth is spacious; so if you do not sincerely worship Me in one land, then sincerely worship Me in another." Then the condition was elided, and in compensation for its elision the object was fronted, with the fronting conveying the meaning of exclusivity and sincerity.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 29, verse 57:

When He commanded His servants to be eager for worship and to take its performance seriously, to the point of seeking out the most suitable lands even if they are far away [[his words "أوفق البلاد وإن شعست" mean "even if they are far away." (ع)]], He followed this with His words ﴿Every soul shall taste death﴾, meaning, experiencing its bitterness and anguish just as the one who tastes something perceives the flavor of what he tastes. Its meaning is: you will all die, and then you will arrive at your recompense. Whoever has this as his end has no choice but to provide for it and to prepare for it with all his effort.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 29, verses 58–59:

﴿لَنُبَوِّئَنَّهُمْ﴾ means "we will certainly lodge them" — that is, "we will certainly cause them to descend" (لننزلنهم) "from the Garden into lofty chambers" (علالي). It is read also as "لنثوّينهم" (we will certainly settle them), from al-thawā' (thawā'), which is alighting in order to dwell.

It is said: thawā fī al-manzil (he dwelt in the dwelling), and athwā huwa (he himself caused to dwell), and athwā ghayrahu (he caused another to dwell). Thawā is intransitive; when it is made transitive by adding the hamza of transference (hamzat al-naql), it does not govern more than one object, as in dhahaba (he went) and adhhabtuhu (I caused him to go).

As for its being transitive to the pronoun of the believers and to the chambers (al-ghuraf), there are two possible ways: either it is treated as being like ﴿لننزلنهم﴾ and ﴿نبوئنهم﴾, or the preposition is omitted and the verb reaches its object directly; or the time-bound place (al-ẓarf al-mu'aqqat) [[Its meaning: the specified/defined one, namely the chambers. (ʿAlī)]] is likened to an indefinite one.

Yahya ibn Wathhab read ﴿فَنِعْمَ﴾ with an added fā'. ﴿الَّذِينَ صَبَرُوا﴾ (those who were patient) — upon leaving their homelands and emigrating for the sake of religion, and upon the harm of the polytheists, and upon trials and calamities, and upon acts of obedience, and abstaining from disobedience; and they relied in all of that upon none but Allah.

When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded those in Makkah who had embraced Islam to emigrate, they feared poverty and loss of livelihood. One of them would say: "How can I go to a town where I have no means of subsistence?" So this was revealed.

"Dābba" (a creature): every soul that crawls upon the face of the earth, whether it has intellect or not.

﴿Many a creature carries not its provision; Allah provides for it and for you.﴾ That is: it cannot bear to carry it, due to its weakness in carrying it. Allah alone provides for those weak beasts, and He alone provides for you, O strong ones, though you are able to carry your provisions and earn them. For if He had not empowered you, nor appointed for you the means of earning, you would be more incapable than the beasts that cannot carry.

From al-Hasan: ﴿carries not its provision﴾ means it does not store it up; it merely rises in the morning, and Allah provides for it.

From Ibn 'Uyaynah: Nothing hoards except humankind, the ant, and the mouse.

From some of them: "I saw the nightingale hoarding in its two wings." And it is said: the magpie has hiding places, but it forgets them.

﴿And He is the All-Hearing of what you say (that is, "We fear poverty and loss of livelihood"), the All-Knowing of what is in your hearts.﴾

The pronoun in "sa'altahum" (if you asked them) refers to the people of Makkah. "Fa-anna yu'fakun" (how are they turned away?) means: how are they diverted from acknowledging the Oneness of God and from not associating anything with Him, despite their acknowledgment that He is the Creator of the heavens and the earth?

Qadara al-rizq wa-qatarahu bi-ma'na idha dayyaqahu (qadara al-rizq and qatarahu mean he restricted it, i.e., when he narrowed it). If you say: the pronoun in His words ﴿and He restricts [it] for whomever He wills﴾ refers to "whomever He wills," so it is as if the extending of provision and its restriction were made for one person. I say: it admits both readings together.

First: he means "and He restricts for whomever He wills," so the pronoun is placed in the position of "whomever He wills," because "for whomever He wills" is indefinite and unspecified, so the pronoun is likewise indefinite, like it.

Second: he means the two matters (extension and restriction) alternate upon one person according to what is beneficial. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knower of all things﴾, knowing what benefits His servants and what corrupts them.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) praised Allah for the fact that he was among those who acknowledged the like of what they acknowledged, and then that this acknowledgment benefited him in affirming the Oneness of Allah and negating rivals and partners from Him. It was not an empty acknowledgment like the acknowledgment of the polytheists. And [He praised Allah] because they acknowledged what is a proof against them, in that they attributed the blessing to Allah while they had made worship directed to the idol. Then He said: ﴿But most of them do not understand﴾ what they say, and what it contains of indication of the falsehood of polytheism and the soundness of Tawhid. Or [it means]: they do not understand what you intend by your saying "All praise is due to Allah," nor do they perceive why you praised Allah upon their saying [it].

This [worldly life] contains a disparaging of this world and a belittling of its affair. And how could it not be belittled, when it does not weigh even the wing of a gnat in His sight? He means: it is merely, because of how quickly it passes away from its people and they die and leave it, like children playing for a while and then dispersing. ﴿And indeed, the Last Abode—that is the [true] life﴾, meaning that there is nothing in it but life that is continuous, enduring, everlasting, with no death [[Mahmud said: "He deviated from the word 'life' (ḥayāh) to this pattern (ḥayawān) to indicate the magnification of the life of the Hereafter and its permanence." Ahmad said: "What is specific to this pattern is that it conveys what does not lack movement, like nazawān (leaping) and jawlān (roaming). And ḥayawān has that quality, and God knows best."]], so that it is, in its very essence, life.

Ḥayawān is a verbal noun (maṣdar) of ḥayy (to be alive). Its regular analogical form (qiyās) would be ḥayyān, and the second yāʾ was changed to wāw, as they said ḥayawa in the name of a man. By it, whatever has life was named ḥayawān (living being/animal). They said: "Buy the dead lands (mawtān) and do not buy the living creatures (ḥayawān)" [[His statement "Buy the dead lands... etc." In al-Ṣiḥāḥ it reads: "Buy the mawtān, and do not buy the ḥayawān." That is: buy the land and the houses, and do not buy the slaves and the animals. (ʿ)]].

The pattern of ḥayawān carries an added meaning not found in the pattern of ḥayāh, namely the meaning of movement and agitation found in the pattern fa‘lān (bina' fa'lan), such as nazawān (leaping), naghaṣān (turbulence) and lahabān (blazing) [[His statement "like nazawān, naghḍān and lahabān": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, lahabān with a vowel on the first letter means the blazing of fire. (ʿ)]], and what resembles these. Life is movement, just as death is stillness, so its coming in a pattern that indicates the meaning of movement is an intensification of the meaning of life. For this reason ḥayawān was chosen over ḥayāh in this place, which calls for emphasis. ﴿If only they knew﴾, so that they would not have preferred the life of this world over it.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 29, verse 65–66:

If you say: With what is the phrase "fa-idha rakibu" (﴿So when they board ships﴾) connected? I say: It is connected with an omitted element indicated by what He described them with and explained of their affair. Its meaning is: They are in the state they were described with, of polytheism and obstinacy, "so when they board ships, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion" (﴿they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾), being in the form of those among the believers who devote religion to Allah, since they mention none but Allah and invoke no other god besides Him. As for calling them "sincere" (mukhlisin), there is a kind of mockery in it. "But when He delivers them to the land, they revert to associating others with Him" (﴿But when He delivers them safely to the land, they associate others with Him﴾). The lam in "li-yakfuru" (﴿so that they may deny﴾) may be the lam of purpose (lam kay), and likewise in "wa-liyatamatta'u" (﴿and so that they may enjoy﴾) for whoever reads it with a kasra. The meaning is: they return to their polytheism so that they, by returning to their polytheism, become ungrateful for the blessing of deliverance, intending only enjoyment and pleasure and nothing else, contrary to the habit of the truly sincere believers: when Allah delivers them, they thank Allah for the blessing of their deliverance and make the blessing of deliverance a means to increased obedience, not to enjoyment and pleasure. The lam may also be the lam of command, and the reading of the one who reads "wa-liyatamatta'u" with sukun (a jussive) supports this. Similar to it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do what you will; surely He sees what you do﴾ (i'malu ma shi'tum innahu bima ta'malna basir). If you say: How is it permissible for Allah, exalted is He, to command disbelief and to command the disobedient to do whatever they wish, while He forbids that and threatens for it? I say: It is a metaphor for abandonment and leaving to oneself, and that the command is one of displeasure up to a limit. An example of this is when you see a man who has resolved upon a matter, and you consider that matter a mistake, leading to great harm, so you strenuously advise him and try to bring him down from his opinion; then when you see from him nothing but refusal and insistence, you become angry with him (hardtu alayhi, meaning: I became angry, as the Sihah states) and say:

"You and your affair; do what you wish," and you do not mean by this the literal command. How could it be, since one who commands a thing wants it, while you are strongly averse and grieved? Rather, it is as if you are saying to him: Since you have refused to accept the advice, you deserve to be told, "Do what you wish," and be left to it, so that it becomes clear to you, once you have done it, that the advisor's opinion was sound and your opinion was faulty.
