Rather, it is as if you are saying to him: Since you have refused to accept the advice, you deserve to be told, "Do what you wish," and be left to it, so that it becomes clear to you, once you have done it, that the advisor's opinion was sound and your opinion was faulty.

The Arabs around Mecca would raid one another, make surprise attacks on each other, and plunder one another, while the people of Mecca dwelt secure and at peace within it. They were not raided, nor were they attacked, despite their small number and the great number of the Arabs. So God reminded them of this particular blessing bestowed upon them, and rebuked them, saying: ﴿Do they believe in falsehood and disbelieve in the blessing of God?﴾ [Qur'an 29:67]. Such an evident and manifest blessing, and others like it, which none can bestow except God alone, are ungratefully rejected by them.

**Their fabrication against God as a lie:** their claim that God has a partner. **Their denial of the truth that came to them:** their disbelief in the Messenger and the Book. In His words ﴿when it came to him﴾ there is a rebuke of them, meaning: they did not hesitate in denying it at the moment they heard it, and they did not act as people of deficient intellect who are cautious in matters do. They hear the report and then apply reflection and thought to it, and they delay until its truth or falsehood becomes clear to them. ﴿Is there not?﴾ is an affirmation (*taqrir*, a statement that compels the listener to affirm a fact) of their dwelling in Hell, like the words of Jarir:

*Are you not the best of those who have ridden the mounts,*
*and the most generous of all the peoples in the palms of the hand?*

These lines are by Jarir about ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwan. The interrogative is for denial, meaning: your superiority in nobility and generosity over all people is not negated. "Those who have ridden the mounts" is a metaphor for them, because riding is among their special privileges. *Rāḥ* is a collective noun whose singular is *rāḥa*, which refers to the part of the palm other than the fingers, and this is a metaphor for generosity, because it is through the palm that kindness is customarily given. It is said that when Jarir reached this verse in the poem, ʿAbd al-Malik was reclining, so he sat up joyfully and said: "This is how we are praised." And he gave him a hundred camels.

Some have said: had it been a genuine interrogative, the caliph would not have given him a hundred camels. Its real meaning is this: the *hamza* (*hamzat al-inkār*, the interrogative particle of denial) entered upon a negation, so it returned to the sense of *taqrīr* (affirmation). Thus there are two readings. The first: "Do they not dwell in Hell, and do they not deserve to dwell in it, when they have fabricated this same lie against God and denied the truth with this denial?" The second: "Has it not become clear to them that there is an abode for the disbelievers in Hell, that they have dared such daring?"

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 29, verse 69:

He left the verb "jahada" (to strive) without an object, so that it would encompass everything that must be striven against: the commanding self (al-nafs al-ammara bi'l-su') and Satan and the enemies of the religion, "fina" (in Us), "fi haqqina" (for Our sake), and "min ajlina" (on account of Us), "wa li-wajhina" (and for Our countenance), sincerely.

﴿And those who strive in Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths.﴾ That is, We will increase them in guidance to the paths of goodness and in success, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance﴾.

And on the authority of Abu Sulayman al-Darani: "Those who strive in what they know, We will guide them to what they do not know." And on the authority of some of them: "Whoever acts upon what he knows, he is granted success regarding what he does not know." It was also said: what we see of our ignorance of what we do not know is only due to our shortcoming in what we do know.

﴿And indeed Allah is with the doers of good﴾, that is, He is with those who help them and support them.

On the authority of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Ankabut, he will have the reward of ten good deeds for every believer and hypocrite." [[Narrated by al-Tha'labi, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Wahidi from the hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka'b.]]
